excerpt_original: Where the Day Begins I believe we all inhabit several temporalities at once: clock time, calendar time, and the rhythm of the domestic space […] Cet article Jenya Kapitsky est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: I believe we all inhabit several temporalities at once: clock time, calendar time, and the rhythm of the domestic space we live in; perhaps also the tempo of places and people woven into our lives; and, finally, our own interior time—each moving at its own pace. It is this interior time that anchors someone to a particular era, whether past or future. I take photographs as I live, and the images form my view of life itself. I am not trying to invent characters or build a conceptual project. The writer and art theorist Viktor Shklovsky wrote that the purpose of art is to “clean the windows”— to restore our ability to perceive the world, to look upon our surroundings with fresh and defamiliarized eyes. Over time, I have taught myself to recognize whatever in the present rhymes with old photographs, with my own inner pace, and with my grandparents’ generation and to photograph it. This draws me toward an imagined world masquerading as “the old days,” with no specific address. It is the kind of time spoken of in Alice in Wonderland: where the day begins; what lingers after a fairy tale has been told or a song sung; what is left of a jar of jam once it has been eaten. It is a time where smiles and memories are kept, a posture, an embrace, a look, and light falling so beautifully it catches your breath. Some of my photographs are taken without ever making an exposure. They exist only in memory—a fleeting moment that dissolved before the shutter could trip, an encounter when I had no camera in hand, or simply a reluctance to break the quiet grace of a scene by moving. Perhaps this imagined time and non-place are a memory of a happy childhood, a longing for a place where no one can return. But either way, what matters to me is creating a space where people can, metaphorically, rest their head on a shoulder, smile, and feel for a moment that this is not only about me and the world around me, but also, a little, about them, and their own happy moments.
